dedupe_keys.name: spaulding rehabilitation hospital boston design for sea level rise and coastal flooding

description: This case study from the U.S. Climate Resilience Toolkit describes how Partners HealthCare designed the Spaulding Rehabilitation Hospital, opened in 2013 in the Charlestown Navy Yard, for flooding and sea level rise. The site sits on a promontory at about current sea level where the Little Mystic Channel meets Boston Harbor; after Hurricane Katrina the owner set voluntary best-practice requirements for the new building. The first floor is 30 inches above the FEMA 500-year flood elevation, all critical infrastructure and patient care are above the first floor so upper floors can stay open if it floods, and switchgear, emergency generators and a gas-fired combined heat and power plant are on the roof. Granite and landscape berms deflect waves, drainage and green roofs shed water, and a triple-glazed shaded envelope with key-operable windows lets patients shelter in place if cooling or heating is lost. Coverage: one hospital in Boston. Access: free web case study. Licence: US government work; photographs are used with permission. Caveats: a narrative by the toolkit, without design calculations. Simulation uses are benchmarks for costing flood-proofing of critical facilities and for passive survivability assumptions in hospital energy and heat models. Related records: the Forde hospital flood protection case study.

outcomes: The first building on the Boston waterfront designed for projected sea level rise, opened in 2013 with its first floor 30 inches above the FEMA 500-year flood elevation, all critical services and plant above the ground floor or on the roof, and resilience measures that added 0.3 to 0.5 percent to construction cost.
